title: Are prompt-to-game tools the future or just hype?
author: Royal_Conflict_9738
selftext: Every few years, something shows up that claims it will “change game development. Remember when drag-and-drop engines were considered revolutionary? Now the conversation seems to be shifting toward AI generation. I saw an example of OneTap Build, where the idea is simple: write your concept → get a playable world. Sounds impressive, but also raises questions. Does faster creation reduce creativity? Or does it actually free creators to focus more on ideas instead of technical setup? Trying to separate real innovation from marketing noise here. What’s your take?

replies.author: CyberDaggerX
replies.body:
I was thinking to myself the other day that video games may be one of the kinds of software for which doing things the old-fashioned way even if AI tools get really good might pay off the most. This is not because of the software aspect of them, but because of the game aspect.

What makes a good game is not something that can be solved with stuff like unit tests and other stuff like that. While that can ensure your game doesn't crash, handling the software side of things, there are many elements to what makes a game gold that are very subjective. Even tabletop games require several rounds of testing and iterative adjustments before being finalized. And the same kind of tests are critical for video game development. Get people to test it, collect feedback, and adjust small elements of the ruleset and game pieces to improve the experience. You will probably want to be able to adjust the knobs of the game individually and precisely to test your theories on how you should proceed, and to do that you should be familiar enough with the code to know where those knobs are. It's not something you can just describe to the AI and trust it'll get right. When you get to the point that you're describing to it the alteration you want it to make in a way that guarantees it'll get it right, it'll be less work to just edit the code directly yourself.

comments.author: SplinterOfChaos
comments.body:
>Does faster creation reduce creativity?

Context: I'm an indie game dev and programmer of 25 years. I'm fascinated by AI and interested in AI communities, but largely skeptical of the software for pragmatic reasons.

I think that this is a really interesting question and it's something that I've actually been trying to talk to people about. When someone tries to learn game development, they generally start following tutorials and end up picking up random advice here and there about coding, art, game design, UI, aesthetics, etc., and you really need to understand all of these topics to some degree in order to create a game people will enjoy. Many devs falter in one area or another and it's typically the area that they haven't explicitly studied.

For example, I see a lot of devs who know that they need professional artwork in order to appeal to their audience, but they struggle to composite the art they receive in their scenes. Even when the art is human-made, I've seen that the incongruencies caused by bad composition can give people an uneasy feeling and lead them to claim it must be done by AI, even when this does not seem to be the case.

When it comes to AI-generated games, they tend to falter in numerous areas, but because the developer doesn't have expertise in them they seem to not recognize what the problems are. After all, if they could see it, they would ask the AI to fix it. And a lot of AI users do, but I suspect those are people who had expertise prior to using AI.

Someone wrote recently in response to "how do I know if my music is good?" that they can ask any one of their friends and most people are a good judge of music and can tell you if they like it or not. An expert will do the same, but they will be able to break down the song structurally and explain precisely what is good or bad about it. 

So I wouldn't really say that it's the fact that people are able to work faster that reduces creativity, but the fact that AI tools take control away from the developer and allow the dev to operate under the assumption that expertise is unnecessary. This isn't a problem with AI, though. As I've pointed out, many devs struggle with this even when using high-quality art made by a human.

I think that prompt-to-game tools are here to stay and you'll always find people using them and wanting more, but I am sleptical that such a tool will ever allow people to produce games of a high enough quality to release on steam or consoles. I think right now there's a lot of hype because people are happy being able to create things when they could not before, but eventually many of them will become dissatisfied with the process.

comments.author: neondaggergames
comments.body:
Neither and both. Haha! The thing I keep thinking is the problem has never been making stuff happen on a screen that LOOKS like a game. It's always, "is this game fun to play?"

Even today the studios with the most talent and endless resources struggle at this exact thing. Most games don't even get to the point where many think they're worth playing. So these tools to my mind can certainly amplify the amount of content that ends up in that pile even if it perfectly emulates where we're currently at with human-grade output.

The other issue is if humans are meant to be kept in the loop (which it appears is going to have to be the case for a while until this problem is solved) how are they going to make better games when entire structures are spit out that will just have to be understood and picked apart in granular detail just to make the game a tight experience?

I think where this makes us end up is a limited use tool even if its' capable of very impressive tech demos that rival human output. It's probably going to be at that state for a long time.

comments.author: Roth_Skyfire
comments.body:
Games are too complex to go down that route and maintain high level of quality. It's already possible to make small scale games that way, it just doesn't create noteworthy results.


Even using solely AI to just write code faces severe limitations due to context limits. It'll work for small scale projects or with lots of manual guidance, but I don't see it doing it all on its own on something big.
